items.title: Title: `AttributeError` in `__repr__` when instantiating unparametrized generic model with `BaseModel` bound
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When a generic Pydantic model uses `BaseModel` as a type hint bound, instantiating the model without parameterization succeeds, but attempting to print or `repr()` the resulting object causes an `AttributeError`.
This appears to be because Pydantic defaults the type to the literal `pydantic.BaseModel` class, which does not have the necessary internal attributes (like `__private_attributes__`) initialized to support Pydantic's internal `__repr__` logic.
Minimal Reproducible Example:
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Foo[T: BaseModel](BaseModel):
    x: T

# Validation succeeds, but the resulting object is "broken"
m = Foo(x={}) 

# This triggers the AttributeError
print(m)
```

Traceback:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "pydantic/main.py", line 1237, in __repr__
    return f'{self.__repr_name__()}({self.__repr_str__(", ")})'
  File "pydantic/_internal/_repr.py", line 62, in __repr_str__
    return join_str.join(repr(v) if a is None else f'{a}={v!r}' for a, v in self.__repr_args__())
  ...
  File "pydantic/main.py", line 1000, in __getattr__
    private_attributes = object.__getattribute__(self, '__private_attributes__')
AttributeError: 'BaseModel' object has no attribute '__private_attributes__'. Did you mean: '__static_attributes__'?
```

Expected Behavior:
Either:
Pydantic should prevent `BaseModel` from being instantiated as a field value during validation.
The `__repr__` logic should be guarded to handle raw `BaseModel` instances without crashing.
Environment:
Python Version: 3.13
Pydantic Version: 2.12.5

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Foo[T: BaseModel](BaseModel):
    x: T

# Validation succeeds, but the resulting object is "broken"
m = Foo(x={}) 

# This triggers the AttributeError
```

items.title: `validate_as` doesn't accept Pydantic's own `Annotated` types (`NewPath`, `FilePath`, etc.)
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`validate_as` works at runtime with `NewPath`, `FilePath`, etc., but the type signature only accepts `type[T]` or `EllipsisType`. 

<details>
<summary>Error (collapsed)</summary>

No overloads for "validate_as" match the provided arguments (Pylance [reportCallIssue](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/blob/main/docs/diagnostics/reportCallIssue.md))

pipeline.py(149, 9): Overload 2 is the closest match

Argument of type "NewPath" cannot be assigned to parameter "tp" of type "EllipsisType" in function "validate_as"

  "Annotated" is not assignable to "EllipsisType" (Pylance [reportArgumentType](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/blob/main/docs/diagnostics/reportArgumentType.md))

</details>


Since Pydantic's own path types are `Annotated[Path, ...]` aliases, they don't satisfy `type[T]`, causing type checker errors. 

Maybe the overload signatures could be broadened to accept annotated types for use in validation chains?


### Example Code

```Python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import FilePath, NewPath, TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import transform

type InputFile = Annotated[FilePath, transform(Path.resolve)]
input_file = TypeAdapter[InputFile](InputFile).validate_python

type OutputPath = Annotated[
    Path,
    transform(lambda p: p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) or p) # make the parent(s)
    .validate_as(NewPath)  # "Annotated" is not assignable to "EllipsisType" (Pylance)
    .transform(Path.resolve),
]
output_path = TypeAdapter[OutputPath](OutputPath).validate_python
```

items.body:
In the `make_field_optional` [example ](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/examples/dynamic_models/) in docs/examples/dynamic_models.md, the `create_model` call uses `type.__name__` to generate the new model's name, but the function parameter is `model_cls`.

This means it references Python's built-in type rather than the passed-in model class, and the generated model always will be named "typeOptional" instead of e.g. "UserOptional":

```python
    return create_model(
        f'{type.__name__}Optional',
        __base__=model_cls,  
        **new_fields,
    )
```

items.title: Spurious Serialization Warnings with List of Discriminated Union
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

I'm seeing unexpected warnings when dumping a **validated** model using `model_dump` and `model_dump_json`. This occurs on a model with a field that is a `list[SomeDiscriminatedUnion]`. See the minimal example below. It is odd that these warnings occur only during serialization, but never during deserialization. 

Presumably this warning serves to warn of a developer error in defining the models or some kind of issue with the model content. Based on the second case below, it doesn't not seem to be an intrinsic issue with the models. However, in all cases, the content is validated. So I would expect all of the code blocks below to serialize without a warning.

Seems like a good candidate for this milestone https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/milestone/13 

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Annotated, Literal, Union

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ModelA(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["A"] = "A"
    value_a: str


class ModelB(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["B"] = "B"
    value_b: int


model_classes = {ModelA, ModelB}

ModelUnion = Annotated[Union[tuple(model_classes)], Field(discriminator="type")]


class ContainerModel(BaseModel):
    model: list[ModelUnion] = Field(default_factory=list)


def validate_and_serialize(container: ContainerModel):
    validated = ContainerModel.model_validate(container)
    return validated.model_dump_json()


# This emits a warning (thus the issue)
container_instance = ContainerModel(model=[])
container_instance.model.append({"type": "A", "value_a": "Hello"})
validate_and_serialize(container_instance)

# This does not emit a warning, so editing the model isn't the problem
container_instance = ContainerModel(model=[])
a_instance = ModelA(value_a="Hello")  # This does not incur a warning
container_instance.model.append(a_instance)

# This does not emit a warning either. Perhaps there is some difference in validation of ContainerModel in `__init__` vs `model_validate`?
container_instance = ContainerModel(model=[{"type": "A", "value_a": "Hello"}])
validate_and_serialize(container_instance)
```

items.title: Stdlib dataclass custom docstrings suppressed from JSON schema description
items.body:
source https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/4138#discussion_r2818450381

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Pydantic suppresses `__doc__` from stdlib dataclasses in JSON schema generation to avoid auto-generated signature docstrings (e.g. `'Foo(x: int = 1)'`) leaking as `description`. However, the suppression doesn't distinguish between auto-generated and custom docstrings — explicit docstrings are also dropped.

This is inconsistent with Pydantic dataclasses, which DO get their custom docstrings included.

The suppression is in `GenerateJsonSchema.dataclass_schema` (`pydantic/json_schema.py`):

```python
if is_stdlib_dataclass(cls):
    # vanilla dataclass; don't use cls.__doc__ as it will contain the class signature by default
    description = None
```

And similarly in `_update_class_schema`:

```python
docstring = None if cls is BaseModel or dataclasses.is_dataclass(cls) else cls.__doc__
```

Python makes it straightforward to distinguish auto-generated from custom docstrings — the auto-generated ones start with `f'{cls.__name__}('`.

This became more visible after #11822 fixed `is_stdlib_dataclass` (previously `is_builtin_dataclass`), which had a bug where dataclasses with `KW_ONLY` sentinel annotations were not recognized as stdlib dataclasses and accidentally got their docstrings preserved.

### Example Code

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = '>=3.10'
# dependencies = [
#     'pydantic>=2.12',
# ]
# ///
import dataclasses

import pydantic
import pydantic.dataclasses
from pydantic import TypeAdapter


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibNoDoc:
    x: int = 1


@dataclasses.dataclass
class StdlibWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


@pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass
class PydanticWithDoc:
    """A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."""

    x: int = 1


print(f'pydantic=={pydantic.__version__}')
print()

for cls in [StdlibNoDoc, StdlibWithDoc, PydanticWithDoc]:
    schema = TypeAdapter(cls).json_schema()
    desc = schema.get('description')
    print(f'{cls.__name__}:')
    print(f'  __doc__     = {cls.__doc__!r}')
    print(f'  description = {desc!r}')
    print()
```

### Output

```
pydantic==2.12.5

StdlibNoDoc:
  __doc__     = 'StdlibNoDoc(x: int = 1)'
  description = None

StdlibWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = None

PydanticWithDoc:
  __doc__     = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
  description = "A custom docstring that should appear as 'description' in JSON schema."
```

**Expected**: `StdlibWithDoc` should also have `description` set since it has an explicit custom docstring.

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```
pydantic version: 2.12.5
python version: 3.13.3
platform: macOS
```

items.title: `typed_dict_schema` JSON schema ignores `extras_schema` when `extra_fields_behavior` is set via config
items.body:
source: https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/4138#discussion_r2814292364

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`GenerateJsonSchema.typed_dict_schema()` correctly uses `extras_schema` to produce typed `additionalProperties` when `extra_behavior` is set as a **top-level** field on the schema, but ignores it when `extra_fields_behavior` is set via the **config** dict — always producing `additionalProperties: true` instead of the typed schema.

This was partially addressed by #10785 / #12123, but only the top-level `extra_behavior` path was fixed. The `config` fallback path (the `elif 'additionalProperties' not in json_schema` branch at the bottom of `typed_dict_schema`) sets `True` without consulting `extras_schema`:

```python
# pydantic/json_schema.py — GenerateJsonSchema.typed_dict_schema()
elif 'additionalProperties' not in json_schema:
    extra = schema.get('config', {a}).get('extra_fields_behavior')
    if extra == 'forbid':
        json_schema['additionalProperties'] = False
    elif extra == 'allow':
        json_schema['additionalProperties'] = True  # <-- ignores extras_schema
```

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic_core import core_schema
from pydantic.json_schema import GenerateJsonSchema

# Top-level extra_behavior — CORRECT
schema_top = core_schema.typed_dict_schema(
    fields={'x': core_schema.typed_dict_field(core_schema.int_schema())},
    extra_behavior='allow',
    extras_schema=core_schema.int_schema(),
)
result_top = GenerateJsonSchema().generate(schema_top)
print(result_top['additionalProperties'])
# {'type': 'integer'} ✓

# Config extra_fields_behavior — BUG
schema_cfg = core_schema.typed_dict_schema(
    fields={'x': core_schema.typed_dict_field(core_schema.int_schema())},
    config=core_schema.CoreConfig(extra_fields_behavior='allow'),
    extras_schema=core_schema.int_schema(),
)
result_cfg = GenerateJsonSchema().generate(schema_cfg)
print(result_cfg['additionalProperties'])
# True ✗ — should be {'type': 'integer'}
```

## Context:
- we have been using `pydantic` as our core component for over 1.5 years now;
- we have deep inheritance hierarchies (up to 5 levels of model inheritance);
- we have heavily nested entity structures (nesting depth reaches up to 8 levels);
- we have large union types that use `Discriminator` (17 entities in the largest union);
- we have large serialized payloads (my initial debug entity was 17k lines of JSON);

### What happened:
After adding an ordinary `field_validator` we had serialization time increased from `0.044` seconds to `183.207` seconds (for the entity of 17k lines), which is about: (183.163 / 0.044) × 100% = **416279%** increase.

Here's a simplified version of the original code that has caused the perfomance issue:
```python
class FooType(StrEnum):
    FOO_ENABLED = "foo_enabled"
    FOO_DISABLED = "foo_disabled"

class InnerTool(BaseModel):
    foo: FooType = FOO_ENABLED

class WrapTool(BaseModel):
    tool: InnerTool
    context_settings: dict[str, Any]

    # START OF NEW CODE:
    @field_validator("tool")
    @classmethod
    def _model_validate_tool(
        cls,
        tool: Tool,
        info: ValidationInfo,
    ) -> Tool:
        # Automatically set context for `InnerTool` in runtime
        context_settings = info.data.get("context_settings")
        if not context_settings:
            return tool

        if isinstance(tool, InnerTool):
            if "foo" in context_settings:
                tool.foo = context_settings["foo"]

        return tool
    # END OF NEW CODE
```

#### What we did after that:
- we discovered the perfomance drop some time later;
- we use `FastAPI`, if was fully blocked while serializing the response and was not responding to any other requests for a few minutes straight;
- unfortunately we had the code untested for some time, so we had to trace back at what commit the perfomance drop had happened;
- then we had to debug what lines of code had caused this behaviour;
- the harderst part was to create an MRE for this, this alone has taken about 10 hours of concentrated work;

## What seems to be the issue:
- the core (?) issue seems to be setting `entity.enum_field = "string_value"` inside `field_validator`;
- but it also happens ONLY if some other model has `@model_serializer(mode="wrap")` overridden (yes, I know it sounds really strange);

### How I have fixed it (temporary solution, perhaps?):
I simply coersed string values to enums.

**Before:**
```python
if "foo" in context_settings:
    tool.foo = context_settings["foo"]
```

**After:**
```python
if "foo" in context_settings:
    tool.foo = FooType(context_settings["foo"])
```

**Result:**
Before `field_validator`: 0.044 seconds;
Without coersion: 183.207 seconds;
With coersion: 0.041 seconds;

## MRE:
Below is the MRE.
The 'base' time for the serialization is 5 seconds (if you just copy and paste the code).
Since there **many** variables that somehow affect this issue, I tried to leave all of them and separate them by 'cases'.
I also couldn't make this any smaller, because it has **a lot of** variables that affect the perfomance...

### Code

```python
# dependencies = [
#     "pydantic==2.12.5",
# ]
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# ///

# ruff: noqa: T201
# ruff: noqa: E501

import copy
import time
from enum import Enum, StrEnum
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Annotated, Any, Final, Literal

from pydantic import (
    BaseModel,
    Discriminator,
    TypeAdapter,
    __version__,
    field_validator,
    model_serializer,
)

    from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

    from pydantic_core.core_schema import SerializationInfo, ValidationInfo

class DataType(StrEnum):
    STRING = "string"
    OBJECT = "object"
    NULL = "null"
    NUMBER = "number"
    INTEGER = "integer"
    BOOLEAN = "boolean"
    ARRAY = "array"

    type: DataType | list[DataType] | None = None
    properties: dict[str, Schema] | None = None

    # CASE1:
    # IF COMMENT OUT `__model_serializer_wrap`:
    # 5s -> Time taken: 0.007714509963989258 seconds
    # Comment: I genually don't know and understand the reason it affects anything, but it does
    @model_serializer(mode="wrap")
    def __model_serializer_wrap(
        self,
        handler: Callable[[BaseModel], dict[str, Any]],
        _info: SerializationInfo,
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return handler(self)

    # CASE2:
    # IF COMMENT OUT `__repr_args__`:
    # 5s -> 4.8-5s
    # Quite insignificant change, but still surprising for me, that's why I left it in the MRE
    def __repr_args__(self) -> Iterable[tuple[str | None, Any]]:
        return (
            (k, v.value if isinstance(v, Enum) else v)
            for k, v in super().__repr_args__()
            if v is not None
        )


# CASE3:
# Core of the issue

# OPTION1 - `StrEnum` + set value is `string`: 5s
# Base case, takes 5 seconds because we set string, not an enum
class MyStrangeEnum(StrEnum):
    ENABLED = "enabled"
    DISABLED = "disabled"


STRANGE_ENUM_DEFAULT: Final[MyStrangeEnum] = MyStrangeEnum.ENABLED
STRANGE_ENUM_OTHER_VALUE: Final[MyStrangeEnum] = "disabled"

# OPTION2 - `StrEnum` + set value is `Enum`: 5s -> 0.0020003318786621094 seconds + [no warnings]
# In this case we operate ONLY with `Enums`, NOT strings
# class MyStrangeEnum(StrEnum):
#     ENABLED = "enabled"
#     DISABLED = "disabled"
#

class InnerTool(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool:inner"] = "tool:inner"
    my_enum: MyStrangeEnum = STRANGE_ENUM_DEFAULT


class WrapTool(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool:wrap"] = "tool:wrap"
    input_schema: Schema
    tool: InnerTool

    @field_validator("tool")
    @classmethod
    def _model_validate_tool(
        cls,
        tool: Tool,
        _info: ValidationInfo,
    ) -> InnerTool:
        # CASE4:
        # IF COMMENT OUT `tool.my_enum=STRANGE_ENUM_OTHER_VALUE`:
        # 5s -> Time taken: 0.0009996891021728516 seconds
        # The main line where the issue happens
        tool.my_enum = STRANGE_ENUM_OTHER_VALUE
        return tool


class ToolType1(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool:type-1"] = "tool:type-1"


class ToolType2(BaseModel):

class ToolType3(BaseModel):

class ToolType4(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool:type-4"] = "tool:type-4"


class ToolType5(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["tool:type-5"] = "tool:type-5"


# CASE5:
# The more entities in a union we have, the more time it takes (exponentially).
# But why, if it should be discriminted by `type` field?

# OPTION1: Union of 7 entities
# 5s
type Tool = Annotated[
    InnerTool | WrapTool | ToolType1 | ToolType2 | ToolType3 | ToolType4 | ToolType5,
    Discriminator("type"),

# OPTION2: Union of 2 entities
# 5s -> 0.8845579624176025s

#     InnerTool | WrapTool,

def gen_json_schema(num_properties: int) -> dict:
    """Generate a JSON schema with the specified number of properties."""

    # Also seems pretty strange for me that it can affect the serialization...

    # OPTION1: ALL TYPES PRESENT:

        {"type": "string"},
        {"type": "integer"},
        {"type": "number"},
        {"type": "boolean"},
        {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},

        prop_type = types[i % len(types)]
        properties[prop_name] = prop_type

    return {

tools_adapter = TypeAdapter(list[Tool])
tool = WrapTool(
    input_schema=Schema(
```

items.title: Tagged union type alias causes validators to run for all union members
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

It seems like using `type Pet = Cat | Dog`, and then using `Pet` instead of `Cat | Dog` directly, causes a change in behaviour of validation of discriminating unions.

### Example Code

A stripped-down version of the official [example](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/unions/#discriminated-unions-with-str-discriminators):

```python
from typing import Any, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator


class Cat(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["cat"]

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def validate_cat(cls, data: Any) -> Any:
        print(f"Validating {cls} with {data}")
        return data


class Dog(BaseModel):
    pet_type: Literal["dog"]

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def validate_dog(cls, data: Any) -> Any:
        print(f"Validating {cls} with {data}")
        return data


class GoodModel(BaseModel):
    pet: Cat | Dog = Field(
        discriminator="pet_type",
    )


print("The good")
GoodModel.model_validate({"pet": {"pet_type": "cat"}})
GoodModel.model_validate({"pet": {"pet_type": "dog"}})
```

The output is as expected:

```
The good
Validating <class '__main__.Cat'> with {'pet_type': 'cat'}
Validating <class '__main__.Dog'> with {'pet_type': 'dog'}
```

But let's suppose I'm using `Cat | Dog` elsewhere, and I want to introduce a name to refer to pets in general:

```python
type Pet = Cat | Dog


class BadModel(BaseModel):
    pet: Pet = Field(
        discriminator="pet_type",
    )


print("The bad")
BadModel.model_validate({"pet": {"pet_type": "cat"}})
BadModel.model_validate({"pet": {"pet_type": "dog"}})
```

The introduction of this alias, which I expected to be a no-op, causes `validate_cat` to be called with an instance of dog data, and vice versa:

```
The bad
Validating <class '__main__.Cat'> with {'pet_type': 'cat'}
Validating <class '__main__.Dog'> with {'pet_type': 'cat'}
Validating <class '__main__.Cat'> with {'pet_type': 'dog'}
Validating <class '__main__.Dog'> with {'pet_type': 'dog'}
```

Note that this doesn't happen if I omit the `type` keyword:

```python
Pet = Cat | Dog
```

Should the union type be resolved from inside the type alias? It seems like it can be obtained through [`__value__`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.TypeAliasType.__value__).

On top of that, pydantic should perhaps throw an error if a `Field` has a `discriminator` set, but is not of a union type. This currently seems to be silently allowed:

```python
class NoErrorModel(BaseModel):
    pet: Cat = Field(discriminator="pet_type")
```

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The ordering of "default" in json schema is inconsistent across runs when the default is an unordered collection (eg: `set`, `frozenset`).

Running the provided code multiple times produces a different schema each time it runs.

My use case is generating a json schema as part of my [bazel](https://bazel.build/) build, but I'm having undesirable behavior due to the generated schema being inconsistent across runs.
In particular, a test that validates that a copy of the json schema that's checked in to source control matches the generated json schema passes locally, but fails in CI (because CI generated a different json schema than what was generated locally).

For example:

```sh
$ diff <(uv run main.py) <(uv run main.py)
20,22d19
<         "a",
<         "b",
<         "f",
24c21
<         "d",
---
>         "f",
26c23,26
<         "e"
---
>         "e",
>         "b",
>         "d",
>         "a"
```

As a workaround, I settled on using `SortedSet[MyEnum]` where `SortedSet` is from [`pydantic_sortedcontainers`](https://github.com/drivendataorg/sortedcontainers-pydantic).

I also considered using the following workaround, but the runtime lie about the type makes me uneasy because `type(MyModel().field) == list`, so code like `MyModel().field.union({MyEnum.A})` would pass the type checker, but would fail at runtime.

```py3
if TYPE_CHECKING:
    _DEFAULT = frozenset(MyEnum)
else:
    _DEFAULT = sorted(MyEnum)

class MyModel(pydantic.BaseModel):
    field: frozenset[MyEnum] = _DEFAULT
```

Finally, I considered the following workaround, but mypy rejects it[^1].

```py3
    field: frozenset[MyEnum] = pydantic.Field(
        default=frozenset(MyEnum),
        json_schema_extra={"default": sorted(MyEnum)},
    )
```

```sh
$ uv run mypy --strict main.py            
main.py:23: error: Dict entry 0 has incompatible type "str": "list[str]"; expected "str": "int | float | str | list[JsonValue] | JsonDict | None"  [dict-item]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```

[^1]: fwiw, this may be a _separate_ `pydantic` bug. I believe this is due to `JsonValue`'s use of `list` (rather than `Sequence`) and `JsonDict`'s use of `dict`, rather than `Mapping`. This causes variance issues when passing a `dict[str, list[str]]`. Shameless plug for https://github.com/cj81499/json_types. See: https://github.com/cj81499/json_types/blob/342e5309b0e37b12cfd9e065d853b018cfee7b47/src/json_types/__init__.py#L18-L20

### Example Code

```Python
import json

import pydantic


class MyEnum(str, enum.Enum):
    A = "a"
    B = "b"
    # strictly speaking, only 2 enum members are required to reproduce, but
    # it is more consistent the more members you have
    C = "c"
    D = "d"
    E = "e"
    F = "f"
    G = "g"


class MyModel(pydantic.BaseModel):
    field: frozenset[MyEnum] = frozenset(MyEnum)


schema = MyModel.model_json_schema()
print(json.dumps(schema, indent=2))
```

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When using Pydantic base models with generic type parameters and some inheritance, attempting to use CloudPickle to serialize these fails with complaints about abstract base class internals:
```python
TypeError: cannot pickle '_abc._abc_data' object
```

This is a regression from Pydantic 2.9 and first appeared in 2.11.0 so far as I can tell.  It is still present in 2.12 and on `main`, at least as of the latest commit at the time of writing (https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic/commit/08b64f7a43f96f02bb0af8d46aba67b3a68d6e88).  While I'm aware that a related issue has been raised with CloudPickle (https://github.com/cloudpipe/cloudpickle/issues/572), the fact that this is a regression on the Pydantic side means I think it is relevant to report here (at least for visibility).

For context, I am testing using Python 3.12, while the aforementioned issue reported by you (@Viicos) against CloudPickle is with Python 3.14.

The reproduction code given below is intended be run as a uv script.

```Python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Foo(BaseModel): ...
class FooWrapper[E: Foo](Foo): ...
```

items.title: Extract type arguments used to specialize generic models at run-time
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://docs.pydantic.dev) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

I've been working on porting a Pydantic V1 [application](https://salsa.debian.org/freexian-team/debusine) to V2, and in the process found myself needing to import from `pydantic._internal._generics`.  Neither my reviewer nor I can think of a better way to do things at the moment, but we agreed it would make sense to file an issue upstream.

A number of parts of our database schema are structured with a category field and some JSON data fields; the category field selects the schema used to parse the JSON data fields.  For example, we have several different kinds of "artifact", each of which has its own schema for "artifact data".  The code to handle each artifact of course wants to work with a validated Pydantic model instance rather than the raw JSON data, but we wanted to keep things reasonably DRY by not repeating the code needed to construct the model in lots of different places.

I invented a pattern that we've found to work well across our application.  When ported to Pydantic V2, it looks something like this (reduced):

```python
import abc
import enum
from types import GenericAlias
from typing import Any, ClassVar, Generic, TypeVar, cast

import pydantic
from pydantic._internal._generics import get_args, get_origin


# The return type is really typing._GenericAlias, but that's private.
def _get_specialization(cls: type, base: type) -> Any:
    """
    Inspect a class for its specialization of a generic base class.

    A class may specialize a generic base class in various ways: for
    example, it might supply specific values for some of the relevant type
    variables, or it might itself be generic and rely on being specialized
    by its own subclasses, or both.  To help us introspect such classes,
    this returns the specialization of `base` by `cls` in the form of a
    :py:class:`typing._GenericAlias`.

    :raises AssertionError: if `cls` specializes `base` in different ways by
      means of multiple inheritance.
    """
    specializations: set[GenericAlias] = set()
    if hasattr(cls, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__"):
        orig_bases = [get_origin(cls)[get_args(cls)]]
    else:
        orig_bases = getattr(cls, "__orig_bases__", [])
    for cls_base in orig_bases:
        origin = get_origin(cls_base)
        if origin == base:
            specializations.add(cls_base)
        elif origin is not None and issubclass(origin, base):
            specializations.add(
                _get_specialization(origin, base)[get_args(cls_base)]
            )
    if len(specializations) != 1:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{cls.__qualname__} must specialize {base.__qualname__} with "
            f"exactly one consistent list of type arguments "
            f"(got {specializations})"
        )
    [specialization] = specializations
    return specialization


def extract_generic_type_arguments(
    cls: type, expected_origin: type
) -> tuple[type, ...]:
    """
    Extract type arguments from a generic class.

    This is expected to be called from __init_subclass__ in a generic class
    (i.e. one that has Generic[...] as a base class), and allows extracting
    the specializing type arguments so that they can be used as factories.
    """
    args = get_args(_get_specialization(cls, expected_origin))
    assert isinstance(args, tuple)
    return args


class ArtifactCategory(enum.StrEnum):
    SOURCE_PACKAGE = "debian:source-package"


class ArtifactData(pydantic.BaseModel):
    model_config = pydantic.ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True, extra="forbid")


class DebianSourcePackage(ArtifactData):
    name: str
    version: str
    dsc_fields: dict[str, Any]


AD = TypeVar("AD", bound=ArtifactData)


class LocalArtifact(pydantic.BaseModel, Generic[AD], abc.ABC):
    """Represent an artifact locally."""

    model_config = pydantic.ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True, extra="forbid")

    category: ClassVar[ArtifactCategory]
    data: AD

    _data_type: type[AD]
    _local_artifacts_category_to_class: ClassVar[
        dict[str, type["LocalArtifact['Any']"]]
    ] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        if get_origin(cls) is not None:
            # The task data type, computed by introspecting the type argument
            # used to specialize this generic class.
            [cls._data_type] = extract_generic_type_arguments(
                cls, LocalArtifact
            )
            LocalArtifact._local_artifacts_category_to_class[cls.category] = cls

    @classmethod
    def create_data(cls, data_dict: dict[str, Any]) -> AD:
        """Instantiate a data model from a dict."""
        return cast(AD, cls._data_type(**data_dict))


class SourcePackage(LocalArtifact[DebianSourcePackage]):
    category = ArtifactCategory.SOURCE_PACKAGE
```

I can think of a few ways that Pydantic might be improved to make this easier, but I'm not sure what would be best:

* `get_args` and `get_origin` could be made public.
* The format of `__pydantic_generic_metadata__` could be documented with some kind of stability guarantee.  (At the moment I wouldn't want to copy the definitions of `get_args` and `get_origin` because they rely on the format of that dictionary, which seems to be private to Pydantic.)
* Perhaps there's some better way of getting hold of type arguments to Pydantic generic models at run-time?  (Note that we also use our `extract_generic_type_arguments` function for cases where the generic class isn't a Pydantic model, so it needs to handle both situations.)

I would like to propose adding a built in `Port` type, similar in spirit to existing network types.

When handling configuration, network ports can be very common. It would be ideal if, when parsing such configuration, ports could be represented in a type safe and semantically meaningful way.

Ports have a clear meaning, and while it can be argued that ports are simply integers with a defined range, this semantic information is currently lost in most model definitions.

items.title: `cloudpickle` issue with models with definitions
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When serializing certain Pydantic models for use in a Spark Connect cluster (using PySpark CloudPickle), the deserialized models are missing their defined attributes.  Attempting to access any of a model's attributes results in an `AttributeError`.

Specifically, this happens when a model is used in more than one attribute of another model, e.g.
```python
class Foo(BaseModel):
    foo: int

class Bar(BaseModel):
    bar1: Foo
    bar2: Foo
```

Deserializing this results in `Bar` being empty.

This happens not just with multiple fields of type `Foo`, but also `list[Foo]`, `list[Foo] | None`, etc.  It is also possible to mix these and observe the same issue, e.g.
```python
class Bar(BaseModel):
    bar1: Foo
    bar2: list[Foo] | None
```

This does not seem to happen when using multiple primitive fields, e.g. the below is fine:
```python
class Baz(BaseModel):
    baz1: int
    baz2: int
```

When running without a Spark cluster and round-tripping through the `CloudPickleSerializer`, the deserialized types are not empty but there are differences in their `__pydantic_serializer__` attribute.  Using `Bar` as defined above, the deserialized `__pydantic_serializer__` attribute looks like:
```
SchemaSerializer(serializer=Prebuilt(
    PrebuiltSerializer {
        schema_serializer: Py(
            0x000000013e13ecb0,
        ),
    },
), definitions=[Prebuilt(PrebuiltSerializer { schema_serializer: Py(0x13e13e7a0) })])
```

Whereas for `Baz` this looks like:
```
SchemaSerializer(serializer=Model(
    ModelSerializer {
        class: Py(
            0x000000013c368340,
        ),
        serializer: Fields(
            GeneralFieldsSerializer {
                fields: {
                    "baz1": SerField {
                        ...
                    },
                    "baz2": SerField {
                        ...
                    },
                },
                computed_fields: Some(...),
                mode: SimpleDict,
                extra_serializer: None,
                filter: SchemaFilter { ... },
                required_fields: 2,
            },
        ),
        has_extra: false,
        root_model: false,
        name: "Baz",
    },
), definitions=[])
```

This is a regression from Pydantic 2.9.2; with everything else in the environment unchanged, deserialization works as expected with Pydantic 2.9.2.
The only changes to the Python environment are:
* `pydantic`, 2.9.2 to 2.12.5
* `pydantic-core`, 2.33.2 to 2.41.5
* `typing-inspection`, 0.4.1 to 0.4.2

The Spark cluster used for testing this update is unchanged apart from having these updated dependencies.

### Example Code

```Python

# dependencies = [
#   "pydantic==2.12.5",
#   "pyspark[connect]==3.5.3",
#   "setuptools==77.0.3",
# ]
# ///

import os
import pydantic as pd
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, types as t

class Foo(pd.BaseModel):
    foo: int

class Bar(pd.BaseModel):
    bar1: list[Foo] | None
    bar2: Foo

class Baz(pd.BaseModel):
    baz1: Foo
    baz2: int

if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]").getOrCreate()

    (
        s
        .range(1)
        .select(
            F.udf(
                lambda: repr(Bar.model_validate_json('{"bar1": [{"foo": 1}], "bar2": {"foo": 2}}'))
```

### Description

SQLAlchemy has two dialects of psycopg: psycopg2 (psycopg package version version 2) and psycopg (psycopg version 3)
The asyncio version of the dialect psycopg (version 3) may also be specified explicitly using the psycopg_async suffix, as:

```
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

asyncio_engine = create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+psycopg_async://scott:tiger@localhost/test"
)
```

https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/dialects/postgresql.html#module-sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.psycopg

items.title: `model_dump()` produces different results when run in empty `contextvars.Context()` - fields missing from generic union members
items.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The result of `model_dump()` depends on the `contextvars` context in which it's executed. When a model containing a union of a base class and a generic subclass is serialized in an empty `contextvars.Context()`, fields from the generic subclass are silently dropped.
This appears to be caused by schema/validator caching in contextvars. When running in a fresh context, the cached schema is unavailable and the regenerated schema incorrectly resolves the union to the base class instead of the generic subclass.

We discovered this issue after uvicorn 0.39.0 changed to [set up fresh contextvars for each request](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/commit/d94bf28743de545d2d4b150f022203a5178cb705). This causes FastAPI/Starlette applications to suddenly produce incomplete JSON responses after upgrading uvicorn, with fields silently missing from serialized models.

### Example Code

```Python
import contextvars
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Base(BaseModel):
    name: str


class Generic[T](Base):
    items: list[T]


class Parent(BaseModel):
    child: Base | Generic[int]


def test():
    return Parent(child=Generic[int](name="x", items=[1])).model_dump()


print("current context:", test())
print("empty context:  ", contextvars.Context().run(test))


**Output:**

current context: {'child': {'name': 'x', 'items': [1]}}
empty context:   {'child': {'name': 'x'}}
```
